doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Great songwriters, standards and Irving Berlin
summary: Pallo listens to jazz and standards on XM and praises songs written by songwriters rather than performers, with a discussion of Irving Berlin playing only black keys.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: In the cars that I’ve been leasing now have XM radio in them, and so we listen to a thing called “Frank’s Place” which plays a lot of nice jazz things, they play John Pizzarelli and Ella Fitzgerald and stuff like that. And I still like to listen to standards, the standards from

the forties up, the real standards. They’re just songs, written by songwriters before the musicians started writing songs. Not that musicians wrote bad songs but you know you had the Lerner and Loewe and all the other ones, they were all great songwriters.
That’s an interesting point you just made. The classic, the standards that never seem to die, like Rod Stewart can—
Come out with—
Three CDs full of these things, and most of those things were not written by performers.

That’s correct. Correct. It was all written by songwriters and that’s all they did. I’m trying to think of them all but Irving Berlin and people like that. Irving Berlin played just the black keys I understand, is that right?
I did hear that. I heard something about he only played in F sharp.
That’s right.
But he had a piano built with some kind of lever on it.
And he changed the keys?
Yeah, it would move, literally move the hammers or some such thing.
That’s what I heard.
I’ve heard that many times.
Wow.
That’s interesting.
They said he played the black keys.
How could he write such great harmonies?

I know, “White Christmas” and “I Lost the Sunshine,” he wrote all those pretty songs he did, a lot of nice things. But the songwriters did write all the good songs from way back. Look at all the old musicals, with Jimmy Cagney, remember he did “You’re a Grand Old Flag,” I’ve forgotten who was the writer.
Oh Cohen.
All right Cohen, you know all them. “Night and Day,” not Cohen but “Night and Day” all those pretty songs, they were all written by songwriters.
